intro: Religion does not stay inside houses of worship. Walk through Chicago and you pass hospitals founded by nuns, food pantries run by mosques, gospel choirs that began on the South Side, and a nine-sided temple on the lakefront in Wilmette. Read the news and you find courts deciding what a public school may do about prayer, and reports of communities driven from their homes because of their faith. This unit follows the world's traditions out into law, art, science, charity, war, peace and the question of freedom.

The first chapter looks at how religions have shaped culture: law codes from Hammurabi's stone to sharia, canon law and the First Amendment; temples, cathedrals, mosques and chant; the long story of religion and science, from the House of Wisdom to Galileo and Darwin; and the giving that traditions call zakat, tzedakah, charity, seva and dana. The second chapter looks at conflict and peace: the Crusades, Europe's wars of religion, the Partition of India and Northern Ireland, and then Gandhi, King, Tutu and interfaith peacemakers, the rights the First Amendment protects, and Chicago's own interfaith history.

By the end of the unit you should be able to explain how a tradition's texts shaped a law, a building or an act of service; describe a conflict in which religion played a part without blaming a whole tradition; explain the Establishment and Free Exercise Clauses; and tell the difference between teaching about religion and practicing it. As always in this course, you will describe and attribute, not judge.
bigQuestion: How have religious traditions shaped the wider world, for building and for breaking, and how can a society keep every faith, and people of no faith, free?

timeline.t: Hammurabi of Babylon has his law code carved on a stone pillar
Pope Urban II calls the First Crusade at Clermont, France
The Roman Inquisition tries Galileo for defending a sun-centered universe
The Peace of Westphalia ends the Thirty Years' War
The First Amendment protects free exercise and forbids an established religion
Charles Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species
The World's Parliament of Religions meets in Chicago
Gandhi leads the Salt March to the sea at Dandi
The Partition of India creates India and Pakistan amid mass migration
The UN's Universal Declaration of Human Rights protects freedom of religion
Clergy of many faiths join the voting rights march from Selma to Montgomery
The Good Friday Agreement largely ends the Troubles in Northern Ireland

words.d: a binding agreement; in the Hebrew Bible, the bond between God and Israel sealed at Sinai
in Islam, God's guidance for all of life, worked out by scholars through fiqh
the internal law of a Christian church, such as the Catholic Code of Canon Law
the avoidance of images of God, people or living beings in religious art
the view that the earth and planets move around the sun
the yearly share of wealth, about 2.5 percent of savings, that Muslims give to those in need
Jewish charitable giving, understood as an act of justice
selfless service in Sikh teaching, seen most plainly in the langar
truth-force; Gandhi's method of open, nonviolent resistance to injustice
the part of the First Amendment that forbids government to establish or sponsor a religion
the part of the First Amendment that forbids government to prohibit the practice of religion
involving people of different religions working or speaking together, each from their own tradition

test.q: How did the rabbis of the Talmud read the law of an eye for an eye?
choices: As a command to injure the offender in the same way
As a rule of fair compensation for the value of the injury
As a law for kings only
As a law cancelled by the Code of Hammurabi
test.why: Jewish tradition read lex talionis as requiring payment equal to the injury, not literal harm.

test.q: Which statement about sharia and fiqh is correct?
choices: Muslim scholars understand sharia as God's guidance and fiqh as the human effort to understand it
Fiqh is the Shia word for sharia
Sharia covers only criminal law
Fiqh is a chapter of the Qur'an
test.why: The ulama distinguish sharia, God's guidance, from fiqh, the human scholarship that interprets it.

test.q: Why are mosques decorated with calligraphy and geometric pattern rather than pictures of people?
choices: Because paint was scarce in Arabia
Because the Qur'an must never be written down
Because of Islamic aniconism, rooted in the Qur'an's rejection of idols and in hadith
Because of the Council of Nicaea
test.why: Islamic art generally avoids images of living beings, so decoration uses Qur'anic calligraphy and pattern.

test.q: Which religious need drove Gregorian chant, cantillation and tajwid alike?
choices: Raising money for charity
Building larger temples
Settling legal disputes
Hearing a sacred text sung or recited correctly
test.why: Each is a way of voicing a sacred text: Christian chant, Torah cantillation and the rules of Qur'an recitation.

test.q: What was Galileo's main argument in his 1615 letter to the Grand Duchess Christina?
choices: That the Bible should be removed from universities
That Scripture teaches how to reach heaven, not how the heavens move
That the earth stands still at the center of the universe
That only Protestants could read the Bible
test.why: Galileo argued that proven facts about nature and a right reading of Scripture cannot truly conflict.

test.q: Which view of human origins do many religious believers call theistic evolution?
choices: The earth is a few thousand years old
Humans evolved with no role for God
Evolution happened as science describes, and God works through it
Each species was created separately in six days
test.why: Theistic evolution accepts the science and holds that God acts through natural processes.

test.q: What does Maimonides rank as the highest level of tzedakah?
choices: Helping a person become self-supporting through a loan, partnership or job
Giving a large gift in public
Giving grudgingly
Giving to a relative
test.why: Maimonides placed enabling someone to no longer need help above every other form of giving.

test.q: Which pairing of practice and tradition is correct?
choices: Zakat - Sikhism
Langar - Sikhism
Tzedakah - Buddhism
Dana - Judaism
test.why: The langar is the Sikh free kitchen; zakat is Muslim, tzedakah is Jewish and dana is Hindu and Buddhist.

test.q: Why do historians say religion was not the only cause of the Thirty Years' War?
choices: Because the war was fought only in the Americas
Because the pope ended it in its first year
Because it began over a trade dispute with China
Because Catholic France paid Protestant Sweden to fight the Catholic Habsburg emperor
test.why: France's alliance with Protestant Sweden shows that power politics outweighed shared faith.

test.q: In the Partition of India in 1947, which communities were caught up in mass migration and violence?
choices: Only Buddhists and Jains
Only British soldiers
Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs
Only the people of Bengal's cities
test.why: Roughly fifteen million Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs crossed the new borders, and violence struck all three.

test.q: What idea did Desmond Tutu use to explain the Truth and Reconciliation Commission?
choices: Satyagraha
Ubuntu, that a person is a person through other persons
Cuius regio, eius religio
Lex talionis
test.why: Tutu drew on ubuntu and on Christian forgiveness; satyagraha is Gandhi's term.

test.q: Which sources did Martin Luther King Jr. draw on for his nonviolent movement?
choices: The Hebrew prophets, the Sermon on the Mount and Gandhi's method
The Code of Hammurabi and canon law
The Qur'an's schools of law
The Peace of Westphalia
test.why: King joined Amos and the prophets and Jesus's teaching on loving enemies with Gandhi's satyagraha.

test.q: A public school principal opens an assembly by leading a prayer. Which clause of the First Amendment does this most likely violate?
choices: The Free Exercise Clause
The freedom of the press
The right to assemble
The Establishment Clause
test.why: School-sponsored prayer is government sponsorship of religion, forbidden since Engel v. Vitale in 1962.

test.q: Why did Congress pass RFRA in 1993?
choices: To create an official national church
To ban peyote in all ceremonies
To respond to the Smith decision by requiring a compelling reason before burdening religious practice
To end teaching about religion in schools
test.why: After Employment Division v. Smith, a broad coalition of faiths asked Congress to restore stronger protection.

test.q: Why do historians call the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions a beginning?
choices: It founded the Bahá'í faith
It was the first formal gathering of the world's religions in the West and helped launch the interfaith movement
It ended the Crusades
It wrote the First Amendment
test.why: Speakers such as Vivekananda and Dharmapala drew American interest, and the modern interfaith movement dates from it.

write.prompt: Should religious communities take part in public struggles over justice, or keep to worship and private life? Cite two or three texts from this unit, such as Amos 5:24, Matthew 25:35-36, Deuteronomy 15:11 or Article 18, and explain what each tradition would say and why.
tips: Name each text you cite with its book and verse, or its article and date.
Attribute every belief to its tradition: Christians hold, the Torah teaches, Gandhi argued.
Show a range of views inside a tradition, such as churches that joined King and churches that opposed him.
Compare the traditions rather than judging which is right.
Use the unit's terms, such as tzedakah, seva, satyagraha and the Establishment Clause.
